subject: Performance SLO qualification - context window & latency impact

Subject: Performance SLO qualification - context window & latency impact

Hi Chris / Alex —

Thanks again for a productive call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we’re aligned on the Performance / SLO items FinCo flagged:

Summary of requirements (as discussed):
- Target latency SLOs: p50 <= 150 ms and p95 <= 350 ms for the most common generation profile (see below).
- Context window: needs to support long docs / conversation state. Primary ask is ~32k-token context for a subset of flows; many calls will be in the 8k–16k range.
- Output token limits: up to 4k tokens for a single response in the long-form workflow; typical responses average ~800–1,200 tokens.
- Throughput & concurrency: steady-state ~150 req/s with peak bursts to 300 req/s; estimated concurrent sessions ~200–400 depending on user behavior.
- Streaming: yes — partial/streamed tokens are required for perceived latency (user-facing streaming).
- Availability/region: US-primary with DR in EU.

Open questions we flagged:
1) Confirm which flows need full 32k context vs shorter windows (we noted the long-form document QA flow as the primary consumer).
2) Expected average input tokens across the mixed workload (you mentioned ~6–8k average for the long-form workloads).
3) Are the p50/p95 SLOs strict for all flows or only the interactive UI flows?

Next steps we propose:
- Redwood will produce a short performance estimate table (p50/p95) for 8k vs 32k context windows and recommended model/quantization configs. (Nikhil will lead).
- Schedule a 2-hour POC run with a small load test (we’ll bring a perf template and run against Dedicated or Hosted as you prefer).
- Share a workbook with detailed token assumptions and cost ballpark.

I’ve attached the SLO readout and a workbook template to collect what FinCo can share on token distributions. If the numbers above look wrong, please correct and we’ll adjust the POC plan.

Thanks —

Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai

Marissa — thanks for the recap and for the attachments. Quick clarifications from our side: 

- The 32k context is required only for the Research/Long-Form QA flow (~20% of traffic). The majority (~60%) will be in the 8k–12k range.
- Average input tokens for the long-form flow are closer to 9k (we were conservative in the call). Outputs average 1.5k but bursts to ~3.5k are possible.
- SLOs: the interactive UI flows (search & snappy answers) are the strict targets (p50 <=150ms, p95 <=350ms). Long-form workflows can tolerate higher p95s (<= 600ms) if streaming is available.

Questions for Redwood: 
1) Can you share expected latency numbers for an 8k vs 32k context window for the model family we discussed (open LLM variant)?
2) What do you recommend for Dedicated vs Hosted for an initial POC?
3) Does Redwood support chunked streaming (i.e., return partial tokens as generated) and how does that affect measured p50/p95?

If you can get Nikhil to share the perf estimates by Monday we’ll populate the workbook and get the procurement folks looped in.

—Chris
Chris Turner
Director, AI Platforms | FinCo

From: Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Performance SLO qualification - context window & latency impact

Hi Chris — copying the perf estimates and recommendations below (high-level). I’ve attached a CSV with the lane-by-lane numbers and assumptions (perf_estimates.csv).

High-level guidance (open-model family, quantized runtime):
- 8k context window (typical interactive flow): p50 ~ 90–120 ms, p95 ~ 220–300 ms (per-request generation to first token + steady stream).
- 16k context window: p50 ~ 130–170 ms, p95 ~ 300–420 ms.
- 32k context window (long-form): p50 ~ 220–280 ms, p95 ~ 450–700 ms depending on model variant and whether KV cache hits are possible.

Notes on streaming/UX:
- Chunked streaming (SSE/HTTP chunked) is supported and typically reduces perceived latency by delivering partial tokens as soon as they are available — users see first tokens ~50–150 ms earlier on average vs waiting for full output. It doesn’t change total compute, but it improves perceived p50 significantly and helps meet UX SLOs for interactive flows.

Throughput & concurrency guidance: 
- For the 150 req/s steady-state (avg tokens per request ~1k–1.5k), a small Dedicated pool (N GPUs) with autoscaling to handle bursts to 300 req/s is recommended. Exact GPU count depends on model variant and quantization; see attached CSV for GPU estimates.
- Continuous batching and KV prefix caching deliver major unit-cost wins; if many requests share recent context, p95 improves.

Dedicated vs Hosted for POC:
- Hosted: fastest to start, we can spin up a dedicated model config in the hosted fleet for the POC. Good for quick validation, but noisy neighbors can affect extreme p95s during burst windows.
- Dedicated: recommended if you need predictable p95 targets for high concurrency (your case for interactive UI SLOs). Dedicated also gives more consistent KV caching and autoscale policies.

Suggested next steps:
1) We’ll provision a small Dedicated test pool (or we can run a Hosted-backed config if you prefer) and run a 2-hour load test simulating the mixed traffic profile you shared.
2) FinCo fills the workbook with token distributions and we’ll map to GPU estimates and cost.
3) We’ll test streaming behavior in the POC so you can validate perceived latency improvements.

Proposed POC schedule: 7/20–7/21 (2 hours of configured load tests + 1 hour of results review). Please confirm availability.

Thanks —

Nikhil Sharma
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
nikhil.sharma@redwood.ai
